newsitem.title: USA: Soybean prices rise on report of stocks plunge.
newsitem.headline: Soybean prices rise on report of stocks plunge.

text.p: The U.S. stockpile of soybeans, a key ingredient in food and livestock production, will shrink to the smallest size in two decades, the government said Friday, heightening concerns over how to stretch supplies until the fall harvest.

In a monthly report, the Agriculture Department also lowered its forecasts of how much corn and wheat would be in U.S. grain bins at harvest time. But it surprised market-watchers by reducing its forecast of soybean supplies by 15 million bushels -- a far larger cut than was expected.

"The big story this month is soybeans," said private consultant John Schnittker. "Soybean prices have to go higher to reduce domestic and export demand. We could anticipate a pretty sharp run-up in bean prices to ration the product enough in the next few months to get by until the new crop comes in."

Only 125 million bushels will be on hand at the end of August, the Agriculture Department forecast. It would be the smallest "stocks" figure since the 1976/77 marketing year and, as a percentage of use, the smallest since 1972/73, when an embargo was put on soybean exports.

Soybean prices initially surged at the Chicago Board of Trade following the report but then fell sharply. Traders said there were signs that high prices were curtailing demand for the popular oilseed, which is used in a wide variety of foods, in livestock rations and in industrial products.
Soybeans sold for $8.30-1/2 a bushel for May delivery on the Chicago Board of Trade, down 24-3/4 cents from Thursday.

Analysts said additional pressure on world supplies came from a cut in the Agriculture Department's estimate in this year's Argentine soybean crop to 13.25 million metric tons from 13.50 million tons, and a corresponding drop in Argentina's bean exports to 1.90 million tons, down from the 2 million tons estimated last month.
Argentina competes with the United States in the global soybean market.

"That soybean stocks number may not stay at the 125 million bushel level," said Mike Hoover, a commodity analyst with the WEFA Group. "There's a limited supply of soybeans out there and huge price strength. I think there's some leeway for that stock number to come back up to 130 or 135 million bushels in the next couple of months."

The monthly report also showed projected U.S. wheat stocks were down 14 million bushels from the previous month's estimate, to 460 million bushels. Wheat imports were estimated to be up 10 million bushels because of a recent surge in imports from Canada, the report said.

Trade relations between the United States and Canada have been strained by North Dakota farmers' fears that Canadian wheat will flood into their markets. The United States has been monitoring Canadian wheat imports since quotas expired in 1995.
U.S. stocks of corn were projected to be down 50 million bushels to 909 million bushels.
Analysts had expected both U.S. corn and wheat stocks to decline, but not by such large amounts.
The monthly supply report also projected that U.S. pork exports this year would soar because of the foot and mouth disease that recently halted all of Taiwan's pork exports.

U.S. exports of pork should reach 1.37 billion pounds in 1997, according to the latest agency estimates. That is up from last month's estimate of 1.1 billion pounds, and nearly double the 771 million pounds exported in 1995.
